newsitem.title: USA: Cuban exiles angered by immigration moves.
newsitem.headline: Cuban exiles angered by immigration moves.

text.p: Angry Cuban exiles demanded on Monday that Washington drop moves to return illegal immigrants to Cuba, calling a plan which would end decades of virtually automatic asylum an "infamy."

U.S. and Cuban officials, in a rare show of co-operation between sworn enemies, met in Havana last week to discuss an accord under which Cubans arriving illegally in the United States could be sent back to the communist-ruled island.

"This is the moment when the Statue of Liberty lets go of her torch and covers her face in shame," said Jose Basulto, president of the Brothers to the Rescue organisation, which plucks so-called "rafters" out of the sea.
Thousands of people risked their lives over the years to flee Cuba, crossing the Straits of Florida in flimsy boats, rafts and even inflated inner tubes.
Unlike illegal immigrants from other countries, they were allowed to stay if they reached the United States.
In Sept. 1994, after a crisis in which 30,000 Cubans tried to cross the straits, Washington and Havana reached a pact under which the United States would issue 20,000 visas a year.
In May this year Washington announced that rafters caught at sea would be returned to Cuba.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Friday that under the plan being discussed any Cuban refugee who entered the United States in violation of its immigration law "is subject to exclusion and return" to Cuba.
Cuban organisations in Miami, the exile capital and bastion of anti-Castro groups, met on Sunday night with Republican Representative Lincoln Diaz-Balart to seek ways of opposing the plan.

"This infamy cannot be accepted by the Cuban people of the diaspora and we demand that the administration of President Clinton withdraw its proposal to return Cuban refugees to Cuba and that it free those refugees currently in detention centres," 26 groups said in a joint statement on Monday.

"The only totalitarian regime remaining in the western hemisphere is the brutal Cuban tyranny and while it exists it is the duty of all brother nations to grant refuge to those who flee its brutality."

The Cuban American National Foundation, whose leader Jorge Mas Canosa is widely believed to covet the Cuban presidency should Fidel Castro's government collapse, called the policy "abhorrent and morally reprehensible".
But the Miami Herald, which usually reflects the views of the exile community, said it was painful but necessary.
Juan Clark, a sociologist at the Miami Dade Community College, said the United States had a right to protect its borders but few stood to gain from any pact.
"The administration claims they haven't changed the policy that people who claim political persecution will not be returned," he told Reuters.
"The problem is nearly everyone there is politically persecuted. The dimension of indirect repression applies to practically everyone."
For Castro it is a double-edged sword, Clark said. In the past he has used migration as a tool to pressure the United States. By closing the escape valve, he may risk a rise in domestic subverison.
Washington's McCurry stressed that Cuban nationals who were now in the United States would not be repatriated.
